title: A city can mandate measurement of algorithmic work impacts before worker outcomes are publicly visible
source_unit: New York City Local Law 25 of 2026 and City Council enactment record concerning a study of algorithmic tools and automated employment decision tools
geography: New York City municipal civil service and algorithmic employment decision context

observations.period: 2026-01-17 enactment; effective 30 days after enactment; current study/report status checked 2026-09-21

denominator.unit: New York City local law and mandated study/report route

institutional_response.value: Local Law 25 of 2026 mandates a Department of Information Technology and Telecommunications study of algorithmic tools and automated employment decision tools

required_scope.value: hiring impacts, impacts on regular employee work functions, and employee feedback

report_requirement.value: report findings and recommendations to the mayor and City Council speaker within three months after study completion

study_report_published.value: not located in the reviewed official public routes as of 2026-09-21

worker_outcome.unit: no named tool, employee decision change, appeal, correction, compensation, workload, pay, or exit endpoint

observations.method: Review of the certified Local Law 25 PDF, City Council enactment record, and NYC DCWP AEDT implementation/complaint page; legal mandate, study scope, and missing report/outcome stages are kept separate.
observations.uncertainty: The law creates a study and report obligation but does not itself establish that a study has been completed, that a report is overdue, that a specific tool affected an employee, or that any worker received protection or remedy.
observations.subgroup: New York City civil-service employees and applicants potentially affected by city algorithmic tools; the law does not publish an exposed-worker denominator.
observations.counterinterpretation: A mandated study may improve administrative visibility and worker voice without changing a hiring, scheduling, evaluation, workload, pay, appeal, or employment outcome.

denominator.unit: New York City Local Law 25 implementation process

coordination_actors.value: NYC Office of Technology and Innovation, Department of Citywide Administrative Services, and Office of Labor Relations

worker_outcome.unit: no worker-level protection, remedy, or employment change identified

observations.method: Official NYC Office of Technology and Innovation testimony recheck, read against the enacted law and existing AEDT implementation context; planning-stage evidence is kept separate from completed-study and worker-outcome evidence.
observations.uncertainty: The testimony reports planning-stage implementation and names coordinating agencies, but does not provide a completed study, public report, instrument inventory, respondent count, completion date, worker notice, appeal, correction, compensation, workload/pay change, or exit endpoint.
observations.subgroup: New York City municipal implementation actors and workers/applicants potentially affected by covered algorithmic tools; no exposed-worker denominator is published in this record.
observations.counterinterpretation: Planning coordination may be an ordinary early implementation step and may later produce useful evidence, but it is not itself worker protection or proof of changed employment conditions.

denominator.unit: joint DCWP, TLC, and CCHR enforcement policy statement

institutional_response.value: The agencies state that entities cannot avoid responsibility for violations of city law because a decision was made or facilitated by AI, algorithmic tools, or other technology

covered_surfaces.value: work, housing, public spaces, consumer transactions, and contracted delivery-worker protections

worker_or_consumer_outcome.unit: no named tool, affected person, complaint resolution, correction, compensation, pay, service, or exit endpoint

observations.method: Review of the official NYC agency policy statement; policy posture is kept separate from a case-level enforcement or remedy outcome.
observations.uncertainty: The statement describes enforcement intent and legal responsibility but does not disclose complaint volume, investigations, violations, tool inventories, worker notice, correction, compensation, or consumer recovery.
observations.subgroup: New Yorkers, workers, consumers, employers, platforms, and agencies within the named city-law domains; no exposed-person denominator is published.
observations.counterinterpretation: A public enforcement posture may clarify accountability without changing a specific algorithmic decision or improving a person's outcome.

denominator.unit: New York City Int. No. 161-2026 reporting proposal

proposed_reporting_fields.value: employees affected, funded positions eliminated, displacement, salary changes tied to changed responsibilities, and employees requiring new training

legislative_stage.value: committee hearing held and matter laid over on 2026-10-05; not enacted

worker_outcome.unit: proposal does not itself report employees, positions, salaries, training completion, remedy, or later employment

observations.method: Review of the official New York City Council legislation record and committee status page; proposed reporting fields are not treated as realized administrative data.
observations.uncertainty: The proposal may change, fail, or be enacted later; the public record does not establish agency reporting compliance, a tool-level inventory, causal displacement, or worker benefit.
observations.subgroup: New York City agency employees and positions potentially affected by reported algorithmic tools; no exposed-worker denominator is published.
observations.counterinterpretation: Adding reporting fields could improve visibility without changing salaries, training quality, job roles, or worker bargaining power.

observations.period: 2026-05-20 and 2026-10-08 introductions; public committee-stage AI complaint architecture

denominator.unit: New York City proposals: Int. No. 919-2026 and Int. No. 1101-2026

proposed_consumer_oversight.value: Int. 919 proposes a DCWP office with an online AI complaint portal, review/referral, consumer advisories, and recommended rules

proposed_civilian_enforcement.value: Int. 1101 proposes investigation of non-frivolous AI complaints and a 25% or 50% share of recovered proceeds for complainants in specified circumstances

enactment_or_outcome.unit: committee-stage proposals; no enacted office, complaint volume, investigation, recovery, or consumer/worker outcome identified

observations.method: Review of official NYC Council proposal records and text; proposed complaint and incentive mechanisms are kept separate from the existing DCWP complaint intake and from realized enforcement.
observations.uncertainty: The proposals may change, fail, or be enacted later; public records do not establish portal operation, complaint counts, investigations, notice of violation, proceeds, or claimant receipt.
observations.subgroup: New York City consumers, workers, and complainants alleging AI-related violations; no complaint denominator or affected-person population is published.
observations.counterinterpretation: A proposed complaint portal or bounty can increase reporting incentives without improving investigation quality, correction speed, restitution, or durable consumer choice.

related_sources.claim: City Council record identifies the enactment date, law number, study scope, and report requirement.
NYC Office of Technology and Innovation testimony reports that the city was in planning stages of implementing Local Law 25 with DCAS and OLR.
NYC DCWP provides the existing AEDT bias-audit, notice, and complaint architecture.
NYC DCWP, TLC, and CCHR issued an October 1, 2026 policy stating that reliance on AI does not remove responsibility under city law.
Int. No. 161-2026 proposes reporting employee displacement, salary changes, and new training associated with algorithmic tools; the October 5, 2026 record shows a hearing and layover, not enactment.
Int. No. 919-2026 proposes an AI oversight office and complaint portal within DCWP.
Int. No. 1101-2026 proposes civilian AI complaints, investigation, and a complainant share of recovered proceeds; the public record shows committee status rather than enactment.

boundary: This record advances the AI/work/consumer chain from rule and complaint architecture to an enacted municipal measurement mandate, reported planning-stage implementation, a citywide AI enforcement posture, proposed employee-impact reporting, and proposed consumer complaint/oversight routes. It does not establish study completion, a published report, named employer or tool implementation, worker notice or appeal, complaint investigation, decision correction, compensation, workload/pay change, trust, or exit.

reproduction_audit.retrieval_hash_scope: Certified Local Law 25 PDF and official City Council records were combined with the October 1, 2026 NYC agency enforcement policy and October 5/8, 2026 legislative-status rechecks
